card.title: Essay 2 — Marriage as a Social Institution (Stephen L. Carter)

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: ## The essay at a glance "Marriage as a Social Institution" by Stephen L. Carter argues against the modern habit of treating marriage as a purely private arrangement between two adults. Carter, a legal scholar, contends that marriage is an **institution** — a publicly defined status with obligations, recognition and meaning that exceed the couple's preferences — and that a society which dissolves marriage into…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Marriage is a commitment institution, not just a private contract — state his thesis.
He argues society benefits when marriage is honoured; note his moral framing.

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Trick 3: His policy angle: making marriage easier to enter and harder to leave (covenant marriage) — quote his proposal for the detail mark.  ·  ## The themes worth an essay **Institution versus private arrangement** — the central theme: the difference between a status conferred by society and a contract invented by two people, and why the difference matters. **Obligation as value** — the conceptual heart: a promise binds only when it means more than the promiser's current preference; the institution's permanence is what gives the vow force.…

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: ## NEB short answers, solved **Q. What does Carter mean by calling marriage a social institution? (2 marks)** A. That marriage is a publicly defined status — with entry rules, social recognition, expected duties and a meaning that outlives the couple's preferences — rather than a purely private arrangement. Society confers the status, and the conferring is what gives the promise its force. **Q.…  ·  ## NEB long answers, solved **Q. "Marriage is a public status, not a private preference." rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Q. Why does Carter call marriage a social institution? (2 marks) — society has stakes in it: stability, children, mutual obligation beyond the couple.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## The argument, step by step The essay opens on the reduction it opposes: the contemporary view of marriage as a private commitment, dissolvable at will, meaningful only to the parties. Carter's first move is definitional: an institution is not a feeling but a structure — with entry rules, public recognition, expected duties and a meaning that outlives any couple's mood.…  ·  ## The devices, with evidence - **Definition as argument** — the essay's master move: the whole case turns on establishing what an institution is, and the definition does the work of the persuasion. - **Dialectic structure** — the reduction stated fairly, then answered: Carter presents the private-commitment view at its strongest before dismantling it, which is why the essay persuades rather than lectures.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Trick 1: Carter's claim: marriage is more than private love — it is a public institution with legal, social and moral obligations; state the thesis.  ·  Trick 2: The two views in tension: marriage as personal choice vs marriage as social commitment — map the essay onto this tension.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Q. What does Carter propose to strengthen marriage? (1 mark) — covenant marriage with stricter entry/exit commitments.
